newsitem.title: USA: Jury asked to find Simpson responsible for murders.
newsitem.headline: Jury asked to find Simpson responsible for murders.

text.p: An attorney dramatically pointed the finger of blame at O.J. Simpson on Tuesday, telling jurors in his civil trial: "There's a killer in this courtroom."

In an impassioned final summation, Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead lawyer, said the voices of Simpson's ex-wife and her friend were speaking "from the grave" and accusing the former football star of being their killer.
Calling Simpson "a guilty man, a man with no remorse, a man with no conscience," Petrocelli exhorted jurors to find him responsible for the June 1994 murders.
He contended that Simpson had offered no explanation for the mass of blood and DNA evidence linking him to the crime and has "lied and lied and lied about every aspect of this case."

Simpson, who was acquitted on Oct. 3, 1995, in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, is now battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families. If he loses, he could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
Closing arguments were expected to be spread out over two days, with the defence likely to get its chance Wednesday and the four-month-old case going to the jury as early as Thursday.

Petrocelli wasted no time lashing into Simpson with a series of harsh accusations. Describing Simpson as a spoiled celebrity with a superiority complex, Petrocelli accused him of weaving a web of lies.

Most dubious, Petrocelli said, was Simpson's denial that he ever owned the kind of Bruno Magli shoes that left bloody prints at the murder scene - testimony that was countered by at least 30 photographs apparently showing him wearing the Italian designer shoes at a 1993 football game.
And Petrocelli contended that contrary to the claims of Simpson's defence team, there was no proof any evidence was planted to frame him.
But the most dramatic moment came when Petrocelli asked jurors to think of the victims.

"The critical pieces of evidence are ... the voices of Nicole and Ron speaking to us from the grave, telling us, telling all of you, that there is a killer in this courtroom," Petrocelli said, pointing at Simpson, seated behind the defence table.
Continuing to jab his finger in Simpson's direction, he declared angrily: "That is the man who confronted them, attacked them and killed them, the defendant, Orenthal (James) Simpson."
Simpson met Petrocelli's attack with a stoic expression, but at other times he became visibly agitated. Some of the victims' family members sobbed quietly at times in the spectators' gallery.
Petrocelli said the victims "in their last struggling moments to stay alive provided us with the key evidence necessary to identify their killer."

He said the glove and knit cap that the attacker left at the murder scene, the fingernail marks and cuts allegedly left on Simpson's hand and the bloody shoeprints that led away from the bodies were ample proof of Simpson's guilt.

Petrocelli said Simpson and his ex-wife had a "classic love-hate relationship" and that when she she upset him, "he hit her time and time again." He claimed Simpson was so obsessed with her that soon after she officially broke off their reconciliation attempt in May 1994, he was driven to murder in a blind rage.
He ridiculed Simpson's claim that he was headed for his ex-wife's grave to commit suicide when he ended up in a low-speed freeway chase leading to his arrest five days after the murders.
"Why does he want to kill himself after he finds out they want to arrest him?" Petrocelli asked in a mocking tone. "Why didn't he kill himself Tuesday or Wednesday?"

When Simpson's lead attorney Robert Baker takes the lectern, he is expected to hammer on a defence theme that proved successful in the criminal case -- that police botched the investigation and planted evidence.

Unlike the criminal trial, which required "proof beyond a reasonable doubt," the plaintiffs in the civil trial will prevail if they can prove there is a 50.1 percent probability - - a "preponderance of the evidence" -- that Simpson committed the murders. And only nine of the 12 jurors' votes are required for a judgment for or against Simpson.
